title: Relative Valuation with Machine Learning

requirements.description: An author-prepared firm-month analysis panel and its required construction inputs for the appendix's traditional-model comparisons, ML targets/predictors, sample splits, valuation-error groups, and portfolio/importance outputs. The appendix specifies 480 monthly cross-sections from January 1980 through December 2019 and some variable formulas; for the v2s equity-value translation it annualizes sales from the current and preceding three saleqt quarters, and it sets missing dltt, dlc, or pstk debt components to zero. It does not provide a complete source-panel schema, firm identifiers, accounting-to-month alignment, full sample rules, the pre-selected random seed, or the remaining construction/input routes. CRSP is named for market equity, but this appendix alone is not a complete source-data specification.

evidence.description: The described machine-learning split covers 480 monthly cross-sections from January 1980 through December 2019 and rotates five firm blocks through test, validation, and training roles.
evidence.quote:
This figure illustrates the split of data into training, validation and test datasets in each of the 480 monthly
cross-sections (January 1980 to December 2019) for machine learning models. Firms in the full sample (as
described in Table 1) are assigned to five blocks using a pre-selected random seed. To generate predicated
target values for all observations, each of the five blocks is used as the test data once. Then, we randomly
choose a validation block from the remaining blocks for machine learning models. The other three blocks are
the training blocks for the machine learning model. In estimating non-machine-learning models, we use four
blocks of data as in-sample data to make predictions for observations in the out-of-sample block. Similarly,
each of the five blocks is used to make out-of-sample predictions once. Five models are trained (fitted in
sample) for each target (dependent) variable using a machine-learning (non-machine learning) model in each
month. A total of 2,400 models are trained (estimated) for each target (dependent) variable.

evidence.description: The appendix names scikit-learn DecisionTreeRegressor and SimpleImputer, median imputation, validation-selected max_depth values from 3 through 6, and a final fit for out-of-sample predictions.
evidence.quote:
We use the DecisionTreeRegressor implementation from the Sci-kit Learn (sklearn) Python package.
This particular implementation cannot deal with missing values. Accordingly we follow the standard advice
(e.g. p. 332 in Hastie, Tibshiranie and Friedman, 2009) and impute missing values with the median value
for each input variable using the SimpleImputer implementation from the same package. It well-known that
trees are prone to over-fitting if grown without limit. We deal with this by choosing the optimal tree depth
(parameter max_depth) for each tree model by evaluating tree depths ranging from 3 to 6 on the validation
dataset. The best performing tree depth on the validation dataset is then used to train the final tree model
and generate out-of-sample test data predictions. (This hyper-parameter tuning process mirrors that used
for choosing the optimal number of trees in the GBM model as explained in Figure IA.1.)

evidence.description: The appendix preserves a robustness branch with an 80/20 train/test split, no validation block, and a fixed 20 trees per model; the base split remains the Figure IA.1 design.
evidence.quote:
Our relative valuation approach is intrinsically cross-sectional. As a result, all observations in
the current month are split into training, validation and test datasets using a 60%/20%/20%
split. This is repeated five times for each month so each observation gets a chance to be in the
test dataset. The approach is described in more detail in Figure IA.1. As a robustness test
we also evaluate an alternative sample splitting method, in which we eliminate the validation
dataset and instead use a 80% training and 20% test split (the approach otherwise remains
the same as explained in Figure IA.1). This means that we cannot determine the optimal
number of trees by evaluating it against the validation set, as we do in our main results.
Instead, we fix the number of trees at 20 for each model. The results are set out in Table IA.6
(see AS_lnm2b, AS_lnv2a and AS_lnv2s – the AS prefix stands for “Alternative Split”).

evidence.description: The equal-observation benchmark includes HP models only from 1989 onward because the appendix says HP data are available only from 1989.
evidence.quote:
GBMs can generate more predictions than traditional models because it does not require all
input variables to have non-missing values to generate a prediction for an observation. In
the main text, we present valuation accuracy based on all the predictions from a model, so
the sample size varies between models. In this section, we report valuation accuracy bench-
marking results when the sample is the same for all models by only considering observations
with no missing predictions from any model (except for the HP models, because HP data
are only available from 1989 onwards).

evidence.description: The appendix defines New Economy firms using a specified three-digit SIC list or an IPO-after-1971/loss-at-IPO rule based on the first post-IPO annual report.
evidence.quote:
These figures compare medians of absolute valuation errors (med(|ε|)) from the three base machine learning
models over time. Panel A reports valuation errors for all firms in the sample (refer to Table 1 for data).
Panel B reports the percentage of New Economy firms across time in the sample. Panels C and D report
valuation errors for New and Old Economy firms across time, respectively. ε is the percentage valuation
error: ε := (M̂ /M ) − 1. M̂ is the predicted equity value and M is the actual equity value. Table 2 provides
model definitions. New Economy firms are either in technology industries (industries three-digit SIC code
of 283, 357, 360-368, 481, 737, and 873) or firms that were IPOed after 1971 and loss-making at the time of
IPO (based on the first annual report available after an IPO). The sample period runs from January 1980
to December 2019.

evidence.description: The appendix's portfolio-results table is equal-weighted, follows the main Table 3 methodology, and excludes stocks below NYSE market-capitalization quantile cutoffs.
evidence.quote:
Table IA.7: Equal-weighted portfolio returns
     This table reports monthly means and abnormal returns of equal-weighted hedge portfolio returns from trading strategies utilising valuation errors.
     This table uses the same methodology as in Table 3 except that strategies in this table are equal-weighted. These equal-weighted strategies exclude
     stocks with market capitalisations below the NYSE quantile cut-offs to mitigate the impact from micro-cap firms.

actions.description: Obtain the author-provided execution materials and complete input/producer specification before attempting the appendix workflow; preserve the appendix's documented branches and do not reconstruct from published result tables.
steps: Request the executable source or, if the authors intentionally provide a manual workflow, the complete ordered procedure and producer-to-consumer handoffs for every appendix branch; identify any author-prepared analysis panel or exact supported source route.

Request the referenced main-text Table 1 sample definition, Table 2 model/variable definitions, Table 3 portfolio methodology, and the pre-selected random seed; specify the firm/security identifiers, record unit, joins, filters, monthly accounting alignment, output fields, and full author panel schema.

For the CRSP market-equity input, map the author's crsp_market_equity measure to a specified monthly CRSP table and adjustment rule. The local catalog lists CRSP.MSF and CRSP.MSF_V2; the latter is readable with PERMNO, MthCalDt, and MthCap in a one-row probe, but the appendix does not establish which product/version, security-to-firm aggregation, field mapping, population, or history is intended.

Resolve the known v2s sales window as current plus the preceding three saleqt quarters and preserve the appendix's missing-debt convention (dltt, dlc, and pstk each zero when missing); request the exact source fields, quarter-to-month match, and any other variable-construction history rather than guessing them.

Request the base GBM implementation, software/version, model settings, and validation search; the appendix names only the CART-side scikit-learn DecisionTreeRegressor/SimpleImputer recipe (median imputation, max_depth 3–6, validation choice and final fit), and specifies 20 trees for the separate 80/20 robustness branch.

Account for the appendix's HP model inputs (available from 1989 only), New Economy rule and required IPO/first-report data, equal-weighted NYSE market-cap cutoff, and FF6 plus seven anomaly-cluster portfolio benchmark inputs; preserve all branches and clarify missing source/producer contracts.
Use the original PDF pages 9–10 as the notation reference for the prediction-to-equity-value formulas if creating working notes; keep those notes separate and do not edit or replace the supplied PDF.
validation: After materials are supplied, compare the author panel's record unit, identifiers, source columns, period/history, formula inputs, and target/predictor fields against the complete author contract; use a bounded metadata probe only for the exact permitted files.

Confirm all appendix analyses and robustness branches have an identified producer, compatible input route, and ordered handoff before any separately authorized run; do not execute estimators as part of this feasibility review.
